title: The Nazirite Vow and the Priestly Blessing
summary: Any Israelite man or woman may take a special vow of separation to the LORD as a Nazirite: no wine or grape products, no cutting of the hair, and no contact with the dead. The chapter explains what to do if the vow is broken by an unexpected death and how to complete it with offerings and the burning of the hair. It closes with the blessing Aaron and his sons are to speak over Israel, placing God's name on his people.
story: The laws of chapter 5 kept the camp from being defiled. Chapter 6 shows the opposite movement: an ordinary Israelite, not a priest or Levite, choosing to draw nearer to God for a season. The camp has tribes on the outside, Levites and priests near the center, and now a way for anyone to step toward that center by a vow. The chapter then ends the long Sinai legislation of Numbers on a note of pure gift. After all the counting, arranging, and guarding, God tells the priests to put his name on the people and promises, “I will bless them” (verse 27). Chapters 7 to 10 will finish the preparations, and then the march begins.
historical:
The Nazirite law assumes that such vows were already known and gives them a form. Later Scripture shows Nazirites in Israel's life. Samson was set apart as “a Nazirite to God from the womb” (Judges 13:5), unusual because his status was lifelong and assigned by God rather than chosen. Hannah vowed that no razor would touch the head of her son Samuel (1 Samuel 1:11). Amos condemns Israel because “you made the Nazirites drink wine” (Amos 2:12). In the New Testament, Paul had his head shaved at Cenchrea to keep a vow (Acts 18:18) and later paid the expenses of four men completing vows at the temple (Acts 21:23-24), which most interpreters take to be Nazirite vows.

The blessing of verses 24-26 is among the oldest biblical texts ever found. Two tiny silver scrolls discovered at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem in 1979, dated to about the late seventh or early sixth century BC, carry a form of these words. They were probably worn as amulets, and they show that the blessing was known and treasured before the Babylonian exile.
cultural:
Each of the three Nazirite rules borrowed a mark of the priesthood. Priests could not drink wine or strong drink when they entered the Tent of Meeting (Leviticus 10:9). The high priest could not go near a dead body, even for his father or mother (Leviticus 21:11), and the Nazirite was held to that same highest standard. The long hair corresponded to the high priest's crown: the word for the Nazirite's consecration, nezer, is also the word for the holy diadem on the high priest's turban. For the length of the vow, an ordinary farmer or a woman of the household lived with something like a high priest's holiness.

The prohibitions were visible and costly. Wine and grapes were staples of daily life and celebration in Canaan, and giving up even raisins and grape seeds meant refusing a common pleasure. Uncut hair marked the vow to everyone who saw it. Corpse impurity, in a world where the dead were washed and buried by their families, meant a Nazirite could not perform the last duties of love for a parent. When the vow ended, the hair was shaved and burned with the peace offering, a meal shared in God's presence, and then the Nazirite could drink wine again.
literary: The chapter has two parts of very different kinds. The Nazirite law (verses 1-21) is case law, carefully arranged: the three prohibitions, each with the phrase about the days of separation; the case of accidental defilement; the ceremony of completion; and a closing summary. The blessing (verses 22-27) is poetry. In Hebrew its three lines grow steadily, from three words to five to seven, and each names the LORD once, so that the divine name is spoken three times. Each line has two verbs, and the second half of each unfolds the first: to bless is to keep, to shine the face is to be gracious, to lift the face is to give peace. The frame around it says what it does. Aaron speaks the words, and God explains that in this way the priests “put My name on the Israelites” (verse 27), and he himself does the blessing.

When the vow is broken by a sudden death
Completing the vow: offerings and the shaved hair

doctrines.note: The Nazirite shows that holiness is not only for the priestly family. Any Israelite, man or woman, could choose to be set apart for a time with a priest's level of devotion. Holiness here means belonging wholly to God, shown in visible, bodily ways.

The blessing reveals what God wants for his people: protection, grace, his favor turned toward them, and peace. It is spoken by priests, but God says, “I will bless them” (verse 27). The blessing is his act, not theirs.

The blessing is a prayer offered on behalf of others, spoken with authority because God commanded it. Jews and Christians have used it in worship for millennia, and it teaches that the heart of prayer for others is asking God to turn his face toward them.

words.note: Nezer, consecration or separation, and also crown. It is the noun behind the Nazirite's title and describes the uncut hair as “the crown of consecration” (verse 7). The same word names the high priest's holy diadem (Exodus 29:6). The Nazirite's hair was his crown, the visible sign that he belonged to God.

Barakh, to bless. To bless in Hebrew thought is to give life, fruitfulness, and well-being, and the word runs from God's first blessing on creation in Genesis 1 to his promise to bless all nations through Abraham. Here God assigns the priests to speak it, but he claims the act for himself.

Panim, face. When God makes his face shine on someone or lifts his face toward them, he looks on them with favor, like a king who turns toward a petitioner and smiles. The opposite, God hiding his face, is a biblical picture of judgment and abandonment. The Psalms echo this line repeatedly, as in Psalm 67:1.

Shalom, peace. It means more than the absence of conflict: wholeness, safety, health, and right relationships with God and others. It is the last word of the blessing and its goal. Everything the blessing asks for arrives here.

christ: Jesus was called a Nazarene because he grew up in Nazareth, not because he was a Nazirite. He drank wine and was accused of being a drunkard (Luke 7:34), and he touched the dead to raise them. John the Baptist, who would “never take wine or strong drink” (Luke 1:15), was closer to the Nazirite pattern. What the Nazirite vow points toward is total, voluntary consecration to God, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the one whose whole life was given over to his Father's will. The blessing has a clearer link. God's face shining on his people finds its fullest expression, in Paul's words, in “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). And Luke's Gospel ends with the risen Jesus acting as a priest: “He lifted up His hands and blessed them” (Luke 24:50). These are fulfillments of a pattern rather than predictions, but the Gospel writer clearly wanted readers to see a priestly blessing in that last scene.

hard.q: Why does the Nazirite need a sin offering when someone dies unexpectedly beside him? How can that be a sin?
hard.a: Verse 11 says the Nazirite “has sinned by being in the presence of the dead body,” even though he could not have prevented it. The Hebrew verb behind sin can mean to miss a mark, and the offering traditionally called the sin offering deals with impurity as well as moral wrongdoing. The scholar Jacob Milgrom argued influentially that it is better called a purification offering, whose purpose is to cleanse the sanctuary and the person from defilement, not to punish guilt. On that reading the Nazirite has done nothing wrong morally, but his vow has been interrupted, and holiness requires that the interruption be dealt with. Others keep the traditional term and stress that the Old Testament recognizes unintentional sins that still need atonement. Either way, the loss of all the previous days of the vow (verse 12) shows that God took the vow seriously, even when the person was not at fault.

questions: The Nazirite vow let ordinary people choose to be set apart for a season. What would a costly, visible act of devotion look like for you, and why might it matter that it is chosen?
The blessing asks that God's face would shine on his people. What difference does it make to picture God looking at you with favor rather than suspicion?
The priests were commanded to bless others. Who could you speak a blessing over this week, and what would you ask God to do for them?
